Are you curious about the latest innovations in medical education and training? Look no further than the exciting rise of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) technologies! These cutting-edge technologies are revolutionizing medical education, offering unique opportunities for medical professionals to learn and refine their skills in a safe and controlled environment.

Welcome to this week's edition of our Digital Health Newsletter! Today we're talking about the exciting rise of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) in medical education and training.

VR and AR technologies offer unique opportunities for medical students, residents, and practicing physicians to learn and refine their skills in a safe and controlled environment. Medical education has traditionally relied on textbooks, lectures, and hands-on experience. Still, VR and AR technologies can offer a new level of interactivity and immersion to help medical professionals better understand complex medical procedures, anatomy, and patient care.

> "The use of virtual reality in medical training is gaining momentum, and it's not hard to see why. VR offers a highly immersive and interactive learning experience that allows students to practice and perfect their skills in a safe and controlled environment." - Dr. Rafael Grossmann, surgeon and pioneer in the use of Google Glass in medicine. (Source: Business Insider)

Research has shown that VR and AR technologies can significantly improve medical education and training outcomes. For example, a study published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research found that medical students who learned surgical procedures using VR had significantly better knowledge retention than those who knew using traditional methods.

One area where VR and AR are handy is surgical training. Surgeons can use VR and AR to practice surgical procedures in a virtual environment, which can help them develop the skills and confidence needed to perform these procedures successfully in real-life situations. For example, Osso VR is a platform that provides immersive surgical training for medical professionals using VR technology.

> "Virtual reality is no longer a gimmick or a game. It is an incredibly useful tool in medical training and education, allowing students to safely practice a wide range of medical procedures and surgeries in a highly realistic environment." - Dr. Justin Barad, orthopedic surgeon and founder of Osso VR, a virtual reality surgical training platform.

In addition to surgical training, VR and AR can be used for patient education. Patients can use these technologies to understand better their medical conditions, treatment options, and surgical procedures, leading to better engagement and adherence to treatment plans. For example, the VR medical education platform, Health Scholars, offers a range of VR and AR modules for patient education.

While VR and AR technologies have great potential for medical education and training, there are still challenges to be addressed. These include issues around the cost and accessibility of these technologies, as well as concerns around the accuracy and reliability of the simulations.

Despite these challenges, the rise of VR and AR in medical education and training represents an exciting development in the field of digital health, with the potential to revolutionize medical education and improve patient outcomes.

Let us know what you think!
building-healthier-world-future-healthca:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/building-healthier-world-future-healthcare-innovation-digital.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

Healthcare is an industry that touches every one of our lives, and it is undergoing a period of rapid transformation. From artificial intelligence and big data to telemedicine and wearable devices, digital health technologies drive innovation and revolutionize how we approach healthcare delivery.

In this newsletter, we will explore the future of healthcare innovation and digital health and how they transform our thinking about healthcare.

Firstly, let's talk about artificial intelligence (AI). AI has the potential to transform healthcare in a multitude of ways. From improving patient outcomes to streamlining administrative tasks, AI is already significantly impacting the industry. AI can analyze vast amounts of medical data, such as electronic health records, to identify patterns and predict patient outcomes. This can help healthcare providers make more informed decisions about patient care and personalized treatments based on individual patient needs.

> "AI is transforming healthcare delivery across the entire spectrum of care, from drug discovery to clinical decision support and patient monitoring." - Dr. Eric Topol, Director and Founder of the Scripps Research Translational Institute.

In the world of digital health, AI has already begun to play a critical role in improving patient outcomes. One of the primary benefits of AI in healthcare is its ability to analyze large amounts of data quickly and accurately. This is particularly important in fields such as radiology, where AI-powered tools can help detect and diagnose diseases faster and more accurately than traditional methods.

Moreover, AI has the potential to personalize patient care. With the help of AI, healthcare providers can identify patterns and trends in a patient's health data, allowing for personalized treatment plans that cater to each patient's unique needs. This customized approach can lead to better outcomes and more efficient use of healthcare resources.

Another area where AI is making an impact on digital health is the development of virtual assistants and chatbots. These tools can provide patients with real-time medical advice, helping reduce the strain on healthcare providers and increase access to care. Additionally, AI-powered chatbots can identify symptoms and recommend appropriate treatments, allowing patients to receive care outside traditional healthcare settings.

However, there are also challenges to be addressed in implementing AI in healthcare. The ethical considerations of using patient data to train AI algorithms and the potential for algorithmic bias are concerns that must be addressed. Moreover, integrating AI into existing healthcare systems requires careful planning and execution to ensure a smooth transition.

Another exciting development in healthcare innovation is the use of big data. Big data refers to large and complex data sets that can be analyzed to reveal insights and patterns. In healthcare, big data can be used to improve patient outcomes by identifying areas for improvement in healthcare delivery and patient care. By analyzing large amounts of data, healthcare providers can identify disease risk factors, track the spread of infectious diseases, and develop personalized treatment plans.

> "The ability to analyze large datasets provides an unprecedented opportunity to improve healthcare outcomes and lower costs." - Karen DeSalvo, former Acting Assistant Secretary for Health in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Telemedicine is also playing a significant role in healthcare innovation. As discussed in our previous newsletter, telemedicine uses digital technology to deliver medical care remotely. It offers increased access, convenience, and improved patient outcomes, particularly in underserved or remote areas. As technology continues to improve, telemedicine has the potential to become an integral part of healthcare delivery, making it easier for patients to receive care from the comfort of their own homes.

> "Telemedicine has been shown to be effective in improving access to care, reducing costs, and improving patient outcomes." - American Telemedicine Association.

Finally, wearable devices are another rapidly evolving digital health area. Wearables, such as smartwatches and fitness trackers, can provide patients with valuable health data, such as heart rate, sleep patterns, and physical activity levels. Healthcare providers can use this data to develop personalized treatment plans and monitor patients' health remotely.

> "Wearable devices have the potential to revolutionize healthcare delivery by providing real-time, continuous health data that can be used to improve patient outcomes." - HealthITAnalytics.

In conclusion, healthcare innovation and digital health are transforming healthcare delivery. AI, big data, telemedicine, and wearable devices are just a few examples of exciting developments in the industry. As technology continues to evolve, the potential for healthcare innovation to improve patient outcomes and build a healthier world is limitless.

Thank you for reading, and please share your thoughts and experiences with healthcare innovation in the comments.
digital-health-pandemic-lessons-learned-:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/digital-health-pandemic-lessons-learned-opportunities-growth.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

As the world continues to grapple with the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, it has become increasingly clear that digital health solutions have played a critical role in mitigating the impact of the virus. From telemedicine to digital contact tracing and remote patient monitoring, technology has enabled healthcare providers to deliver care safely and effectively in the face of unprecedented challenges.

But beyond its immediate benefits, the pandemic has also revealed key lessons about the state of digital health and the opportunities for growth in this rapidly evolving field. Here are a few key takeaways from the past year:

Telemedicine is here to stay.

One of the most significant changes wrought by the pandemic has been the rapid adoption of telemedicine. With in-person visits limited by social distancing measures, healthcare providers and patients alike have turned to video consultations and remote monitoring to maintain continuity of care.

While telemedicine has been around for years, its widespread use during the pandemic has highlighted the need for more investment in the infrastructure and technology needed to support it. As such, we can expect to see continued growth in this space, as more providers incorporate telemedicine into their practices and more patients become comfortable with virtual visits.

Data is key.

Another critical lesson from the pandemic has been the importance of data. From tracking the spread of the virus to identifying high-risk populations and monitoring patient outcomes, data has played a central role in our response to the pandemic.

Moving forward, we can expect to see continued investment in data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) to help healthcare providers make more informed decisions about patient care. In particular, AI-powered tools like predictive analytics and personalized treatment algorithms hold enormous potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs.

Remote monitoring is the future of chronic disease management.

The pandemic has also highlighted the need for better tools to manage chronic conditions remotely. With many patients unable or unwilling to visit healthcare facilities in person, remote monitoring solutions have become increasingly important for managing conditions like diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

As such, we can expect to see continued investment in remote monitoring solutions, including wearable devices and mobile apps that enable patients to track their own health metrics and share that information with their care providers.

Digital health is an essential component of public health.

Perhaps the most significant lesson from the pandemic has been the importance of digital health as a critical component of public health. From contact tracing apps to vaccine distribution systems, technology has played a central role in our efforts to contain and control the spread of the virus.

As such, we can expect to see continued investment in digital health infrastructure, including public health data systems and interoperability standards that enable seamless communication between different healthcare providers and public health agencies.

In conclusion, while the COVID-19 pandemic has been a challenging and difficult time for healthcare systems around the world, it has also highlighted the enormous potential of digital health solutions. From telemedicine to remote monitoring and data analytics, technology has played a central role in our response to the pandemic and will continue to be a critical tool in our efforts to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs in the years to come.
from-echis-go-data-digital-health-improv:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/from-echis-go-data-digital-health-improving.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

Imagine a world where digital technologies and data are used to improve health and well-being for everyone. A world where health systems are efficient and sustainable, delivering good quality, affordable and equitable care. A world where innovation and transformation are driven by digital health solutions that leverage ubiquitous technologies such as mobile phones, internet, and cloud computing. This is not a distant dream, but a realistic possibility for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) that face multiple health challenges.

Digital health is the use of digital technologies and data to improve health and well-being. Digital health can help make health systems more efficient and sustainable, enabling them to deliver good quality, affordable and equitable care. These high ideals are challenging to attain, especially for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) that face multiple health challenges, such as infectious diseases, maternal and child mortality, malnutrition, mental health, and non-communicable diseases.

However, digital health also offers great opportunities for innovation and transformation in LMICs. By leveraging ubiquitous technologies such as mobile phones, internet, and cloud computing, digital health can enhance access to health information and services, empower health workers and communities, strengthen health surveillance and response, and enable data-driven decision making.

In this issue, we will highlight some examples of how digital health is making a difference in low-resource settings around the world.

In Ethiopia, the Electronic Community Health Information System ([eCHIS](https://www.moh.gov.et/site/projects-3-col/echis)) is a mobile platform that digitizes the paper-based Community Health Information System (CHIS), one of the backbones of Ethiopia’s successful health extension program.

![Image by Ministry of Health (MoH)](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/362f396c9e86b3e0.jpg)
*Image by Ministry of Health (MoH)*

[eCHIS](https://www.moh.gov.et/site/projects-3-col/echis) enables health extension workers (HEWs) to collect, manage, and use data about community-level health services, as well as to communicate and coordinate with health centers. [eCHIS](https://www.moh.gov.et/site/projects-3-col/echis) also provides HEWs with job aids and guidance to improve their service delivery and performance. [eCHIS is currently implemented in over 4,000 health posts and health centers across Ethiopia(1)](https://www.moh.gov.et/site/projects-3-col/echis)

The [mHero](https://www.mhero.org/) platform in Liberia is a two-way communication system that connects health workers and health authorities using mobile phones. The platform allows health authorities to send targeted messages to health workers based on their location, role, or skill set, and to receive feedback and data from them.

![Image by Trevor Snapp for IntraHealth International](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/9abed96e40a527f2.jpg)
*Image by Trevor Snapp for IntraHealth International*

The platform also supports health worker training, supervision, and motivation. [mHero was developed in response to the Ebola outbreak in 2014 and has since been used for various health programs, such as immunization, maternal and child health, and COVID-19 response(2)](https://www.mhero.org/)

The [MomConnect](https://www.health.gov.za/momconnect/) program in South Africa is a national mobile service that provides pregnant women with free maternal health information and advice via SMS or WhatsApp. The program also allows women to interact with health professionals and provide feedback on the quality of care they receive at public health facilities.

![Image by MomConnect](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/05fdf6f7b722ff85.jpg)
*Image by MomConnect*

The program aims to improve maternal and child health outcomes, as well as to strengthen the health system through data collection and analysis. [MomConnect has reached over two million women since its launch in 2014(3)](https://www.jnj.com/our-giving/momconnect-connecting-women-to-care-one-text-at-a-time)

In 2019, WHO launched a tool called [Go.Data](https://www.who.int/tools/godata) to track outbreaks in real-time. [Go.Data](https://www.who.int/tools/godata) is a web-based platform that allows field teams to collect and analyze data on cases, contacts, laboratory results, and epidemiological links during outbreaks.

![Image by OpenWHO](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/ed6ff305fb06541e.jpg)
*Image by OpenWHO*

The platform supports data visualization, geolocation, network analysis, and interoperability with other systems. [Go.Data](https://www.who.int/tools/godata) [has been used in several outbreaks, including COVID-19(4)](https://www.who.int/tools/godata)

These are just some of the examples of how digital health is contributing to the response to COVID-19 and other health challenges in LMICs. To learn more about digital health initiatives around the world, you can visit the WHO’s [digital health website](https://www.who.int/health-topics/digital-health/) or read the [best practices in scaling digital health in LMICs](https://globalizationandhealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12992-018-0424-z).

That’s all for this week’s issue of the Digital Health Digest. Stay tuned for more updates on digital health innovations around the world. Thank you for reading and subscribing!

Dear Subscribers,

Welcome to our weekly Digital Health LinkedIn Newsletter, where we explore the latest trends and technologies in the field of digital health. This week, we delve into the crucial topic of healthcare interoperability and standardization efforts.

![No alt text provided for this image](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/e28f1048dc4cde8d.jpg)

In order to facilitate seamless communication and data exchange between various healthcare systems, providers, and devices, interoperability, and standardization are essential. To ensure that healthcare information can be shared reliably, securely, and effectively, common frameworks, protocols, and data formats must be established.

💡 Interoperability is crucial for improving patient care, boosting operational efficiency, and enabling improved health outcomes in the contemporary healthcare environment where data is generated from diverse sources such as electronic health records, wearable devices, and telehealth platforms. Here are a few essential elements of healthcare.

🌟 Data integration and exchange: Healthcare interoperability strives to make it easier for data to be integrated and transferred between various platforms and systems. This entails making sure that authorized healthcare practitioners can easily access and share health information, such as patient records, test findings, and medication histories. In order to make better-informed decisions and coordinate care, healthcare personnel need to be able to examine the patient's health information holistically.

🌟 Regardless of the electronic health record (EHR) systems used by healthcare organizations, health information exchange (HIE) activities are focused on creating secure networks and standards for sharing patient data among them. These projects seek to break down data silo barriers and facilitate the safe sharing of patient data, encouraging collaboration and continuity of care between various providers.

> The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) states that "interoperability is critical to the success of electronic health records (EHRs) and other health information technologies (IT) because the availability of secure, accurate, and complete patient health information at the point of care is essential to providing safe, effective, and efficient patient-centered care."(1)

🌟 The establishment of standards and procedures for healthcare interoperability is being worked on by a number of organizations and initiatives. These include SMART on FHIR, Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise (IHE), Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), and Health Level Seven International (HL7). To enable the uniform transmission of health information, these organizations offer frameworks, specifications, and guidelines.

🌟 Governments and regulatory authorities are making efforts to recognize the value of standardization and interoperability in healthcare. They are putting into effect laws and policies that support data sharing, interoperability, and patient access to their medical records. For instance, the Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, which requires healthcare providers to share patient data electronically, ensures seamless information flow and patient empowerment. It was introduced by the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

In conclusion, initiatives to standardize and increase healthcare interoperability are crucial for smooth data interchange, greater care coordination, and improved patient outcomes. We can break down data silos, facilitate effective collaboration, and realize the full potential of digital health technologies by developing standard frameworks, protocols, and data formats.

I hope you found this week's Digital Health LinkedIn Newsletter informative and insightful. Stay tuned for more updates on the latest trends in digital health.

References:

Welcome to our weekly Digital Health Digest Newsletter, where we bring you the latest trends and technologies in the field of digital health. This week, we are excited to explore the potential applications of blockchain technology in healthcare.

Blockchain technology is an innovative solution that has been gaining traction in recent years due to its decentralized nature, security, and transparency. It offers a distributed ledger system where data can be stored securely without a central authority, making it ideal for industries that require high-level security and transparency.

In healthcare, blockchain technology has the potential to revolutionize the industry by improving the security, privacy, and efficiency of patient data management, clinical trials, and supply chain management. Let's delve into some potential applications of blockchain in healthcare.

One of the most significant applications of blockchain technology in healthcare is the secure sharing of patient data. In traditional healthcare systems, patient data is stored in centralized databases that are vulnerable to hacking and data breaches. With blockchain technology, patient data can be stored in a decentralized, tamper-proof, and transparent distributed ledger system. This means that patients can control their data and grant access to healthcare providers and researchers without compromising their privacy.

Blockchain technology can also streamline the clinical trial process by providing a secure and transparent platform for managing data. Clinical trials involve the collection of large amounts of data from patients and healthcare providers, which can be time-consuming and costly to manage. Blockchain technology can simplify the process by providing a secure and transparent platform for storing and sharing data. This can reduce the time and cost of clinical trials, improve patient recruitment, and enhance data accuracy.

Another potential application of blockchain technology in healthcare is supply chain management. Medical devices, drugs, and other healthcare products are subject to strict regulatory requirements and quality standards. Blockchain technology can improve the efficiency of supply chain management by providing a transparent and secure way of tracking the movement of products from manufacturers to distributors, and ultimately to patients. This can prevent counterfeiting, reduce waste, and ensure the safety and quality of products.

> According to a report by Deloitte, "the use of blockchain can create a secure and interoperable platform for patient data exchange and facilitate more comprehensive and efficient patient care."

While blockchain technology is still in its early stages of adoption in healthcare, there are several ongoing initiatives and partnerships exploring its potential. For example, Philips, the healthcare technology company, is collaborating with the blockchain-based platform, BurstIQ, to explore the use of blockchain in healthcare data management.

In conclusion, blockchain technology has the potential to transform healthcare by improving the security, privacy, and efficiency of patient data management, clinical trials, and supply chain management. As more healthcare providers and organizations adopt blockchain technology, we can expect to see significant improvements in patient outcomes and healthcare delivery. Stay tuned for more exciting developments in the world of digital health.

We hope you found this week's Digital Health Digest Newsletter informative and engaging. Don't forget to subscribe to our newsletter for the latest updates on digital health.

state-of-ai-ethiopian-healthcare-2025:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/state-of-ai-ethiopian-healthcare-2025.jpg?v=mwboiy08)
*Regional adoption rates across Ethiopia's federal regions. Explore the [interactive dashboard](https://appaipy-ggv5p4sbemcayf8a2b8rwz.streamlit.app/) for the full picture.*

Artificial intelligence is reshaping healthcare worldwide. For Ethiopia, a nation of more than 120 million people carrying a dual burden of infectious and chronic disease, AI promises a way to stretch scarce resources and widen access to care. How that promise translates into clinical reality has, until now, been largely unmapped.

This landscape analysis surveyed **449 healthcare professionals** (doctors, nurses and midwives, public health officers, pharmacists and IT specialists) across 13 regions and city administrations, to see how ready the workforce is for that transition.

## Three findings

- **The knowledge-practice paradox.** More than 75% of respondents correctly identified basic AI definitions, yet knowledge barely predicts use (r = 0.14). Education is no longer the main bottleneck; infrastructure is.
- **The anxiety curve.** A third of the workforce (33%) fears being replaced by AI. That anxiety is often higher among specialist physicians and PhD holders than among junior staff.
- **Innovation beyond the capital.** Adoption is not confined to Addis Ababa. Sidama shows surprisingly intense adoption, which points to the potential for regional centres of excellence.

## How the study was done

The survey followed the Knowledge, Attitude and Practice (KAP) model:

- **Knowledge:** understanding of AI definitions, ethics and limitations.
- **Attitude:** optimism about AI against fear of displacement.
- **Practice:** how often AI tools are used, which ones, and whether their outputs are checked.

Respondents were reached through professional networks (LinkedIn, Telegram and medical associations), so this is a convenience sample: 449 validated responses after cleaning, from Addis Ababa, Oromia, Amhara, Sidama, Somali, Tigray, Southern and Central Ethiopia, Harari, Dire Dawa, Afar, Benishangul Gumuz and Gambella. The analysis used Python (Pandas, Plotly, GeoPandas) for correlation, geospatial clustering and sentiment analysis.

## Knowing about AI: the literacy illusion

Ethiopia's health workforce is past the stage of simply not knowing what AI is. But much of that knowledge is shallow:

- **The ethics gap.** Some respondents who were confident about AI definitions were unsure about its ethical implications. This is "buzzword literacy": knowing the term *machine learning* without grasping its statistical dependencies or its potential for bias.
- **Diagnosis before treatment.** Confidence is much higher in AI for diagnosis (radiology, pathology) than for treatment planning, which mirrors where AI tools are most mature globally.

## Feeling about AI: hope and fear at once

Attitudes swing between strong optimism and real worry:

- **Efficiency against displacement.** Most agree AI will reduce administrative burden, yet about 33% fear it will eventually replace physicians.
- **The expert paradox.** Specialists are the most anxious, perhaps because diagnostic expertise is exactly what AI aims to replicate.
- **A call for regulation.** About 86% want strict government regulation. In Ethiopia, regulation is seen not as a brake but as a precondition for trust.

## Using AI: the practice gap

- **Polarised use.** The heaviest users tend to be younger, urban men; non-users are concentrated where infrastructure is weakest.
- **Shadow IT.** High use in places with little official digital infrastructure suggests health workers are turning to personal phones and consumer tools such as ChatGPT for clinical questions. It is resourceful, but it carries real risks for patient privacy and safety.
- **Automation bias.** Some of the heaviest users said they rarely or never verify AI outputs. Blind trust in an algorithm is a latent clinical risk, especially for drug doses and interactions.

![Bubble chart of knowledge against trust in AI by professional role](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/ai-ethiopia-2025-knowledge-vs-trust.png)
*Knowledge against trust, by role. Bubble size reflects the number of respondents.*

## Where AI is taking hold

The data challenges the idea that digital health in Ethiopia begins and ends in the capital. Sidama, perhaps helped by regional health initiatives and Hawassa University, stands out. In Afar and Somali, respondents show strong enthusiasm, a kind of "digital hunger", but low practice: AI is seen as a way to fill specialist gaps, and infrastructure is what holds it back.

## What should change

More teaching about what AI is now brings diminishing returns. Four shifts would do more:

1. **Infrastructure first.** Move investment from awareness workshops to subsidised data and verified hardware. Access is the strongest predictor of practice.
2. **Teach AI hygiene.** Train clinicians to question and verify AI outputs, not just to use the tools.
3. **Back regional innovation.** Recognise and fund emerging hotspots like Sidama, so tools are tested in diverse settings rather than only in Addis Ababa.
4. **Keep humans in the loop.** The Ministry of Health should state clearly, in policy, that AI augments clinicians rather than replaces them.

## Read the full report

- Full report (PDF), with DOI: [doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17792784](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17792784)
- [Interactive dashboard](https://appaipy-ggv5p4sbemcayf8a2b8rwz.streamlit.app/)
- [Code on GitHub](https://github.com/abelMest/AI-in-Healthcare-Ethiopia) (MIT licence)

Participant data has been anonymised and aggregated; the raw dataset is not public. The report is published under a CC BY 4.0 licence.

**Cite as:** Mekonnen, A. M. (2025). *The State of AI in Ethiopian Healthcare: A 2025 Landscape Analysis*. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17792784
digital-health-needs-operating-system:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/digital-health-needs-operating-system.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

I have been in a lot of digital health launches. A new system goes live, a ribbon is cut, a photo is taken in front of a laptop in a district hospital. Everyone means it.

Then I go back a year or two later. Sometimes the system is running well. Often it is not. The server has stopped. The trained staff have moved on. The donor grant ended and nobody budgeted for the licence. Or the system works, but it cannot talk to the three other systems in the same facility, so a nurse types the same patient into each of them.

None of these failures is about technology. The software usually did what it promised. What failed was everything around it.

## We have strategies. We lack a way to run them.

Africa does not suffer from a shortage of plans. Most of our countries have a digital health strategy. We have good global guidance: the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the Global Digital Health Monitor, OpenHIE, the Principles for Digital Development, and Africa CDC's own work on digital transformation. These documents describe what good looks like, and they describe it well.

What they cannot do is tell a digital health lead what to do on Monday morning. Who has the authority to stop a duplicate project? What should a contract say about who owns the data? When is a pilot ready to scale, and who decides? How do you keep a system running after the partner leaves? How should a ministry decide whether an AI tool is safe to use?

These are operating questions. In most places they are answered person by person, project by project, and the answers leave when the people do.

## Why an operating system

A computer has hardware and it has apps. Neither is much use without the operating system that makes them work together, decides what runs and when, and keeps things stable when something goes wrong.

A health system has its own hardware and apps: devices, connectivity, software, data. It also has people, money and rules. Digital Health OS is the layer that makes them work as one: the decisions, roles and routines that turn a collection of projects into a system.

![Digital Health OS: nine modules in three layers. Direct: governance, strategy and investment. Build: architecture, data, products, AI. Run: people, implementation, measurement. Evidence from measurement feeds the next plan.](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/digital-health-os-map.png)

I think of it in three layers.

**Direct** is where direction is set. It covers governance (who decides, and how) and strategy and investment (one costed plan that every funder aligns to, including the running costs nobody likes to pay).

**Build** is the shared foundation every service runs on. It covers architecture and standards, data, how products are bought, and now AI.

**Run** is where it becomes real in facilities. It covers people and skills, implementation from pilot to national scale, and measurement that proves the investment was worth it.

That makes nine modules in three layers, with one loop that matters most: what we measure should change the next plan and the next budget. When that loop works, a system learns. When it does not, we repeat the same pilot in a new district every few years.

## What makes it different

I am not proposing another framework to sit next to the others. The OS is built to be practical, and it rests on three commitments.

**Practical over aspirational.** Every module ends in something a team can do this week: a checklist, a template, a decision rule. If it cannot be acted on, it does not belong.

**Built on what exists.** The OS points to the global frameworks rather than replacing them. In the same spirit, it asks countries to reuse and connect national systems before buying new ones.

**Written from implementation.** The lessons come from real rollouts in Ethiopia and across the continent, including the ones that did not work. We learn as much from a stalled project as from a successful one, and we rarely write the stalled ones down.

## The weakest module sets the pace

The most useful idea in the OS is also the simplest. A system is only as mature as its weakest module.

A country can have excellent architecture and still stall because nobody has the authority to say no to a duplicate system. An organisation can have strong data and still fail because there is no budget to keep the servers on. The goal is not perfection everywhere. It is to find the module that is holding the rest back, and to fix that one first.

That is why the first thing I am building is a short self-assessment. It covers nine modules with three questions each, scored on a five-level maturity scale. It is honest about where you are, and it points you to the module to work on next.

## What comes next

Over the coming weeks I will publish one module at a time here on Digital Health Digest, starting with governance, architecture and implementation. Each piece will set out what good looks like, the common pitfalls, and a few tools you can use straight away. After that comes the self-assessment, free for any ministry, organisation or team that wants to use it.

I want this to be shaped by the people who do the work. If you lead digital health in a ministry, a hospital, an NGO or a startup, tell me which module keeps you up at night. Tell me where the frameworks stopped being useful. Tell me about the project that should have scaled and did not.

We have spent a decade proving that digital health can work in Africa. The next decade is about making it work routinely, everywhere, and for longer than one grant cycle. That is what an operating system is for.
clinical-decision-support-systems-new-er:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/clinical-decision-support-systems-new-era-digital.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

In the world of healthcare, even the smallest decision can have life-changing consequences. Should a patient be prescribed a certain medication? What are the odds of a certain diagnosis? While medical school prepares doctors for a lot, the complexity and pace of modern healthcare mean that clinicians now have a powerful new ally: Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS).

Imagine a digital assistant—like Siri, but for healthcare. CDSS leverages artificial intelligence to analyze mountains of data, from lab results to a patient’s medical history, offering real-time recommendations that help guide everything from diagnoses to treatment plans. And the timing couldn’t be better. As the global healthcare industry rapidly digitizes, CDSS is emerging as an indispensable tool, offering the potential to transform not only the speed and accuracy of care but also patient safety and overall health outcomes.

How CDSS is Already Helping Hospitals

CDSS are designed to assist healthcare providers in making informed clinical decisions by analyzing vast amounts of data, including patient history and lab results. This technology enhances diagnostic accuracy and treatment effectiveness, which aligns with the article's assertion that CDSS can transform healthcare delivery. According to the [Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality](https://www.ahrq.gov/cpi/about/otherwebsites/clinical-decision-support/index.html), CDSS tools provide timely information at the point of care, helping reduce medical errors and improve patient outcomes.

![npj Digital Medicine (](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/li/a4c4a1ee693a9b9e.jpg)
*npj Digital Medicine (*

CDSS comes in two main types: Knowledge-Based, using set medical guidelines, and Non-Knowledge-Based, which leverages AI and machine learning to detect patterns. These tools are particularly valuable in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, tailoring treatments, and improving patient safety. For example, CDSS can alert clinicians to potential drug interactions, reducing medication errors—a leading cause of patient harm.

Clinical Decision Support Systems are already active in major health institutions across the world, becoming as essential to doctors as stethoscopes. In the emergency room at some facilities, for instance, CDSS algorithms review patient scans and alert radiologists to potential issues—whether it's spotting subtle signs of a stroke or flagging an area of concern on a lung X-ray. This digital second-opinion can catch what even the best human eyes might miss, particularly during high-stress shifts.

Over in the oncology department at one university, another CDSS tool helps personalize treatment for cancer patients. By cross-referencing individual patient data, like genetic markers and lifestyle factors, the system can suggest chemotherapy treatments more likely to succeed for each specific patient. Doctors are finding that these data-driven recommendations don’t just optimize treatment—they give patients a new level of confidence in their care.

And then there’s another example, where CDSS is helping surgeons and anesthesiologists monitor high-risk surgeries. In real-time, these tools track vital signs and issue alerts about any unusual fluctuations that might indicate complications. With this extra set of “digital eyes,” clinicians can take proactive steps when every second counts.

Why CDSS Could be a Game Changer for Patients, Too

For patients, the benefits are already becoming clear. CDSS promises greater accuracy in diagnoses, especially in resource-limited settings. In clinics across India, for example, CDSS has been deployed to help non-specialist providers make reliable diagnoses for conditions like tuberculosis and pneumonia. With limited access to specialists, these clinics are able to provide quality care that would have otherwise required a lengthy—and sometimes impossible—referral process.

But perhaps the biggest leap is happening in patient safety. In the United States alone, medication errors are a persistent issue, often due to drug allergies, dosage errors, or dangerous drug interactions. By embedding CDSS into electronic health records (EHRs), hospitals are seeing fewer of these errors. The system flags potential risks before they reach the patient, ensuring that clinicians are alerted to any red flags they might have missed in the rush of their rounds.

What’s Standing in the Way?

Despite its promise, widespread CDSS adoption faces some significant hurdles. First, the quality of the data is paramount: Without accurate, standardized, and timely data, CDSS can’t function optimally. Unfortunately, healthcare systems often rely on a patchwork of EHRs that don’t “speak” to one another, leaving critical information fragmented. Recent interoperability standards in the U.S. and Europe are setting the groundwork to change this, but there’s a long road ahead.

Then there’s the matter of trust. Not all clinicians are ready to welcome CDSS into their practice. For some, these systems can feel intrusive, even undermining their expertise. Hospitals like Mount Sinai in New York are addressing this by providing extensive training on CDSS and emphasizing that the tool doesn’t replace their judgment—it enhances it.

And, as with any tool that handles sensitive patient information, privacy concerns are paramount. In an age of data breaches, it’s essential that CDSS comply with stringent privacy regulations, like HIPAA in the U.S. and GDPR in the EU, to protect patient information.

Where CDSS is Headed Next

If the current trajectory holds, CDSS could soon become as common in hospitals as stethoscopes or blood pressure cuffs. Researchers are exploring ways to deepen CDSS’s capabilities, such as using natural language processing to scan and interpret doctors’ notes for more contextual insights. Meanwhile, AI advances will only improve the predictive accuracy of these systems, potentially leading to CDSS that can offer recommendations with even greater precision.

In lower-resource areas, where access to doctors is limited, mobile-based CDSS is expected to make a big impact. Imagine a smartphone app that helps healthcare workers make better-informed decisions on the spot—a powerful tool for bridging healthcare gaps in rural or underserved communities worldwide.

Why It Matters

Clinical Decision Support Systems aren’t just a new technology; they represent a fundamental shift in how we think about healthcare. By combining human expertise with AI’s analytical power, CDSS offers a smarter, more precise, and potentially more equitable approach to medicine. For the healthcare industry, CDSS could be one of the most transformative tools of this era, ensuring that the best possible care is no longer just about what one doctor knows, but about what the world’s collective medical knowledge can deliver.

As healthcare continues to evolve, the question may not be if CDSS will become widespread, but rather, how quickly it will reshape the field. From big-city hospitals to rural clinics, CDSS is already changing the way healthcare is delivered—and it’s only just getting started.

![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/ethiopia-digital-health.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

Digital health in Ethiopia is in its early stages of development, with comparatively low levels of access and usage. There are increasing efforts to expand the digital health sector, but significant challenges remain to ensure equitable access across the population. The government has explored several initiatives to expand digital health services, such as the Mobile Health Information System, which provides public health data through mobile phones, and e-Health Ethiopia, which is a centralized platform for hosting patient records. These initiatives have had mixed results and have yet to be fully integrated into mainstream healthcare delivery. Digital health networks are still nascent and medical infrastructure remains largely fragmented, contributing to wide disparities in access.

EMR in Ethiopia is developing rapidly. The Ethiopian government has made a significant commitment to improving access to electronic health records (EHRs) and digital health services. As of 2019, over 70% of primary healthcare facilities across the country had some form of EMR system, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). However, many of these EMRs are not connected, making it difficult for patients to share their medical information between providers. In addition, there are still many barriers preventing health workers from efficiently using EMRs, such as limited technical training and inadequate financing.

### What obstacles are there to the use of EMR in Ethiopia?

1\. Cost: The cost of implementing an electronic medical record (EMR) system in Ethiopia is very high due to the lack of resources available, limited government funding and the presence of foreign suppliers with high prices.

2\. Data Security: Many employers and healthcare professionals in Ethiopia are wary of using EMR due to concerns over data security, as any breach in patient information could potentially have major implications.

3\. Lack of Training: Ethiopian healthcare providers often do not have enough training on how to use the technology safely or securely, resulting in inadequate utilization of such systems and hampering their effective implementation.

4\. Infrastructural Deficiencies: Poor Internet coverage and inadequate bandwidth also hinder EMR adoption in Ethiopia as these issues restrict access to information stored remotely in the cloud for many Ethiopians.

5\. Cultural Issues: Perception issues regarding technology also exists among many health practitioners and citizens which limits its overall acceptance and use hindering EMR uptake throughout the country.

### What should we do next?

1. Raise Awareness: Education plays an important role in improving health outcomes. Raising awareness of the benefits that digital health can bring to Ethiopia is key, including efforts to better inform individuals of the advantages newer technologies have over traditional health services. 

2\. Modernize Healthcare Infrastructure: It is essential that Ethiopia begin modernizing its healthcare infrastructure by introducing Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) into its policies and health systems so as to provide up-to-date and efficient services to citizens. 

3\. Collaborate with Partners: Governmental and non-governmental organizations should collaborate to build a stronger, more unified platform for digital health in Ethiopia through investing in shared resources such as data platforms, digital tools, and research initiatives. 

4\. Research & Development: Research and development related to digital health should be promoted within the country in order to further understand how best to use technology for improving public health outcomes in Ethiopia. 

5\. Support Funding & Investment: Governments, international institutions, civil society organizations, private sector businesses must all play an important role in funding improvements which are necessary for successful uptake of digital healthcare tools in Ethiopia. Funders must understand the needs of those using these services so that the right support is made available through the right channels
digital-health-enterprises-comprehensive:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/digital-health-enterprises-comprehensive-overview.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

Hello everyone,

Imagine a world where you can consult with your doctor without leaving your home, manage your health metrics at your fingertips, and have your health data seamlessly integrated across different healthcare providers. Sounds like a dream, right? But this is not a dream anymore, it’s the reality of Digital Health Enterprises!

Digital Health Enterprises are organizations that provide digital healthcare management solutions for providers and patients. They use technology to deliver better, faster, and cheaper services that improve health outcomes and quality of life. In this article, we will explore the main aspects of Digital Health Enterprise Architecture, such as standards, workforce, monitoring and evaluation, platform, and applications. We will also explain why they are essential for the success and sustainability of digital health enterprises.

### Standards: The Foundation of Digital Health

Standards are the rules and guidelines that define how digital health systems and services should operate and interact. They ensure interoperability, quality, and safety of digital health solutions. They also facilitate data exchange, integration, and analysis across different platforms and applications.

Some of the key standards that are relevant for digital health enterprises are:

- HL7 FHIR: A standard for exchanging health information electronically. [It enables interoperability between different systems and devices, and supports a variety of use cases, such as clinical care, research, public health, and quality improvement](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/overview.html).
- ISO 13606: A standard for representing and communicating electronic health records. [It defines a common information model and terminology for health data, and supports semantic interoperability and data reuse](https://www.iso.org/standard/67868.html).
- DICOM: A standard for storing and transmitting medical images. [It enables the integration of medical imaging devices, such as X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs, with other systems and applications, and supports image analysis and diagnosis](https://www.dicomstandard.org/about).

Standards are essential for digital health enterprises because they:

- Enable communication and collaboration among different stakeholders, such as providers, patients, researchers, and policymakers.
- Enhance the quality and efficiency of digital health services, by reducing errors, duplication, and waste.
- Improve the safety and security of digital health solutions, by ensuring data privacy, integrity, and availability.
- Support innovation and scalability of digital health solutions, by enabling interoperability and compatibility among different platforms and applications.

However, adopting and implementing standards in the healthcare sector is not without challenges. Some of the challenges are:

- Lack of awareness and knowledge of existing standards and their benefits among healthcare professionals and organizations.
- Lack of alignment and coordination among different standards development organizations and initiatives.
- Lack of incentives and resources for healthcare providers and organizations to adopt and implement standards.
- Lack of regulation and enforcement of standards compliance and quality assurance.

To overcome these challenges, digital health enterprises need to:

- Educate and train their staff and partners on the importance and use of standards.
- Collaborate and coordinate with other stakeholders and initiatives to harmonize and promote standards adoption and implementation.
- Provide and seek incentives and resources to support standards adoption and implementation, such as funding, technical assistance, and recognition.
- Follow and comply with the relevant regulations and policies on standards and quality assurance, such as accreditation, certification, and auditing.

### Workforce: The Engine of Digital Health

Workforce capacity building is the process of developing and enhancing the skills and competencies of digital health professionals. It includes education, training, mentoring, and career development. It also involves creating and maintaining a conducive and supportive work environment and culture for digital health professionals.

Some of the skills and competencies that are required for digital health professionals are:

- Technical skills: The ability to use and manage digital health technologies, such as software, hardware, and devices. This includes skills such as programming, data analysis, system administration, and cybersecurity.
- Clinical skills: The ability to provide and improve digital health services, such as telemedicine, remote monitoring, and digital therapeutics. This includes skills such as diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and education.
- Soft skills: The ability to communicate and collaborate effectively with different stakeholders, such as patients, providers, and partners. This includes skills such as empathy, teamwork, leadership, and problem-solving.

Workforce capacity building is vital for digital health enterprises because it:

- Improves the performance and outcomes of digital health services, by ensuring quality, efficiency, and effectiveness.
- Enhances the satisfaction and retention of digital health professionals, by providing opportunities for learning, growth, and recognition.
- Increases the demand and supply of digital health services, by creating awareness, trust, and loyalty among customers and partners.
- Fosters innovation and sustainability of digital health solutions, by enabling creativity, adaptation, and improvement.

However, developing and retaining digital health talent in the healthcare sector is not without challenges. Some of the challenges are:

- Lack of awareness and recognition of the value and role of digital health professionals among healthcare professionals and organizations.
- Lack of standards and accreditation for digital health education and training programs and providers.
- Lack of opportunities and resources for digital health professionals to access and participate in digital health education and training programs and activities.
- Lack of incentives and support for digital health professionals to pursue and advance their digital health careers.

### Platform: The Heart of Digital Health

A digital health platform is a software system that provides the core services and functions of digital health solutions. It enables the integration and interoperability of different digital health applications and devices, and supports the delivery and management of digital health services. It also facilitates the collection and analysis of data and information on digital health solutions.

Some of the services and functions that a digital health platform provides are:

- Authentication: The process of verifying the identity and credentials of users and devices that access the digital health platform and services. It ensures the security and privacy of digital health solutions, and prevents unauthorized access and misuse.
- Communication: The process of exchanging data and information among users and devices that use the digital health platform and services. It enables the collaboration and coordination of digital health providers and patients, and supports various modes of communication, such as voice, video, text, and chat.
- Service delivery: The process of providing and receiving digital health services through the digital health platform and applications. It enables the delivery of various types of digital health services, such as telemedicine, remote monitoring, digital therapeutics, and health education.
- Service management: The process of managing and optimizing the performance and quality of digital health services through the digital health platform and applications. It enables the management of various aspects of digital health services, such as scheduling, billing, reporting, and feedback.
- Data collection: The process of collecting and storing data and information from users and devices that use the digital health platform and services. It enables the collection of various types of data and information, such as health records, vital signs, symptoms, and behaviors.
- Data analysis: The process of analyzing and interpreting data and information from users and devices that use the digital health platform and services. It enables the analysis of various types of data and information, such as trends, patterns, correlations, and predictions.

A digital health platform is the heart of digital health enterprises because it:

- Connects and integrates different digital health applications and devices, creating a seamless and comprehensive digital health ecosystem.
- Supports and enhances the delivery and management of digital health services, improving the accessibility, affordability, and quality of healthcare.
- Facilitates and enables the collection and analysis of data and information, generating insights and evidence for digital health improvement and innovation.

However, developing and maintaining a digital health platform in the healthcare sector is not without challenges. Some of the challenges are:

- Lack of interoperability and compatibility among different digital health applications and devices, creating silos and fragmentation of digital health solutions.
- Lack of scalability and reliability of digital health platform and services, resulting in performance and quality issues and customer dissatisfaction.
- Lack of security and privacy of digital health platform and services, exposing data and information to risks of breaches and misuse.
- Lack of regulation and compliance of digital health platform and services, creating legal and ethical issues and liabilities.

To overcome these challenges, digital health enterprises need to:

- Adopt and implement standards and guidelines for digital health interoperability and compatibility, such as HL7 FHIR, ISO 13606, and DICOM.
- Design and develop scalable and reliable digital health platform and services, using cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and blockchain technologies.
- Implement and enforce security and privacy measures for digital health platform and services, such as encryption, authentication, and consent management.
- Follow and comply with the relevant regulations and policies for digital health platform and services, such as HIPAA, GDPR, and FDA.

### Applications: The Hands and Feet of Digital Health

Digital health applications are software programs that provide specific solutions and features for digital health services. They run on different devices, such as smartphones, tablets, computers, and wearables, and interact with the digital health platform and other applications and devices. They offer a wide range of services, from facilitating virtual consultations to managing health metrics and symptoms remotely.

Some of the types of digital health applications are:

- Telemedicine applications: Applications that enable virtual consultations between patients and providers, using voice, video, text, or chat. They allow patients to access healthcare services from anywhere, anytime, and reduce the cost and time of travel and waiting. They also allow providers to reach more patients, especially in remote and underserved areas, and improve the efficiency and quality of care.
- Remote monitoring applications: Applications that enable remote monitoring of patients’ health status and conditions, using sensors, devices, and data. They allow patients to track and manage their health metrics, such as blood pressure, glucose, and heart rate, and receive alerts and feedback. They also allow providers to monitor and intervene in patients’ health situations, and prevent complications and hospitalizations.
- Digital therapeutics applications: Applications that enable digital delivery of therapeutic interventions, using software, devices, and data. They allow patients to receive personalized and evidence-based treatments, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, medication adherence, and lifestyle coaching. They also allow providers to prescribe and monitor digital therapies, and measure their effectiveness and outcomes.
- Health education applications: Applications that enable health education and awareness, using content, media, and gamification. They allow patients to learn and improve their health knowledge, skills, and behaviors, such as nutrition, exercise, and stress management. They also allow providers to educate and empower their patients, and improve their health literacy and engagement.

Digital health applications are the hands and feet of digital health enterprises because they:

- Reach and serve different segments and needs of customers, creating a diverse and inclusive digital health market.
- Provide and improve different types of digital health services, creating a comprehensive and holistic digital health system.
- Collect and generate different types of data and information, creating a rich and valuable digital health resource.

However, developing and using digital health applications in the healthcare sector is not without challenges. Some of the challenges are:

- Lack of usability and accessibility of digital health applications, creating barriers and difficulties for customers to use and benefit from them.
- Lack of evidence and validation of digital health applications, creating doubts and concerns about their effectiveness and safety.
- Lack of adoption and utilization of digital health applications, creating gaps and disparities in digital health service delivery and outcomes.
- Lack of regulation and compliance of digital health applications, creating legal and ethical issues and liabilities.

To overcome these challenges, digital health enterprises need to:

- Design and develop user-friendly and accessible digital health applications, using user-centered design, user testing, and user feedback.
- Test and evaluate the effectiveness and safety of digital health applications, using randomized controlled trials, clinical trials, and real-world evidence.
- Promote and encourage the adoption and utilization of digital health applications, using marketing, education, and incentives.
- Follow and comply with the relevant regulations and policies for digital health applications, such as FDA, CE, and MDR.

### Conclusion: Join the Digital Health Revolution!

As you can see, Digital Health Enterprises are revolutionizing healthcare by providing better, faster, and cheaper services to patients and providers. They are also creating new opportunities for innovation, collaboration, and growth in the healthcare sector.

But how can you be part of this digital health revolution? How can you leverage the power of Digital Health Enterprises to improve your health, your business, or your career?

Whether you are a patient, a provider, or a professional, I have the right advice for you. And I want to share it with you.

That’s why I invite you to subscribe to my newsletter “Digital Health Digest”. In this newsletter, you will learn:

- The latest trends and best practices in digital health
- The key challenges and opportunities for digital health enterprises
- The proven strategies and solutions for digital health success
- The real-life case studies and testimonials from our clients and partners

The newsletter is free and open to anyone who is interested in digital health. All you need to do is to subscribe to my newsletter at [abelmest.substack.com](http://abelmest.substack.com)🔔 to stay informed and get the latest updates delivered straight to your inbox.

Don’t miss this chance to join the digital health revolution and take your health, your business, or your career to the next level.
harnessing-digital-health-essential-skil:
![](https://divchzdusulnetgulnwk.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/photos/editions/covers/harnessing-digital-health-essential-skills-transforming-healthcare.jpg?v=mwboiy08)

A few years ago, as a healthcare professional deeply committed to improving patient outcomes, I found myself standing at a crossroads.

The healthcare field was evolving, and digital health was rapidly becoming more than just a buzzword.

However, the challenges faced by developing nations like those in Africa and other parts of the world added layers of complexity to this evolution.

For healthcare professionals in these regions, the journey into digital health is not just about staying relevant—it’s about overcoming systemic barriers, leveraging limited resources, and driving innovation in contexts where the stakes are incredibly high.

In today’s rapidly evolving healthcare landscape, digital health is no longer a futuristic concept but a present-day reality.

This is true even in regions where infrastructure challenges and resource constraints create unique hurdles.

The rise of telemedicine, electronic health records, AI-driven diagnostics, and wearable technology is opening new doors for healthcare delivery in developing nations, but it also underscores the critical need for health professionals who are not only clinicians but also tech-savvy innovators.

What skills do health professionals in these contexts need to thrive in the digital health arena?

Here’s a guide to the essential competencies that can set you apart in this dynamic field, particularly in developing regions.

### Technical Proficiency with Local Context Awareness

Imagine being a healthcare provider in a rural clinic in sub-Saharan Africa, where the nearest hospital is miles away and electricity is intermittent.

One day, you receive a patient who needs specialized care that your facility cannot provide. In the past, this situation might have resulted in a tragic outcome due to the lack of immediate resources.

But today, armed with a tablet and a solar-powered battery, you can connect with a specialist hundreds of miles away through a telemedicine platform.

This isn't a futuristic scenario—it's a reality for many health professionals in developing regions who are creatively leveraging digital health tools to bridge the gap between limited resources and quality care.

Understanding and working with digital tools and platforms is fundamental for health professionals everywhere, but in developing regions, it often requires an added layer of creative problem-solving.

The challenges of limited internet connectivity, unreliable power supply, and outdated infrastructure demand that health professionals not only understand these tools but also adapt them to fit local realities.

For instance, a clinician in Kenya might need to use an electronic health record (EHR) system that operates offline and syncs data only when connectivity is available.

Similarly, telemedicine platforms may need to function with low-bandwidth options to ensure consultations can take place even in areas with poor internet coverage.

Familiarity with data management and cybersecurity principles is crucial, especially in environments where digital infrastructure may be less robust. In regions where cybersecurity measures might not be as advanced, health professionals must be vigilant in protecting patient information.

This could mean adopting low-tech solutions for high-stakes problems, such as using secure paper records as a backup or ensuring that data stored on local devices is encrypted and password-protected.

For example, in some countries, health workers have been trained to use mobile health apps that track patient data even in remote locations.

These apps are designed to work offline and upload data only when a connection is available, ensuring that patient information is both accessible and secure.

The ability to adapt these tools to the local context, ensuring they function optimally despite infrastructural limitations, is a testament to the ingenuity required in these settings.

Protecting patient information remains a top priority, but the methods to achieve this often need to be adapted to local realities. In some areas, health professionals may need to rely on a combination of digital and analog systems to ensure that patient data is not only secure but also accessible when needed.

This might involve developing protocols for securely transferring data between mobile devices and centralized databases or training staff on the importance of data privacy in environments where such practices are not yet the norm.

In conclusion, technical proficiency in digital health is not just about understanding the latest tools—it's about knowing how to apply them effectively in the unique and challenging environments of developing regions.

Health professionals must be both innovative and pragmatic, finding ways to harness the power of digital health technologies while adapting them to the realities of their local context.

This combination of technical skill and contextual awareness is what enables them to deliver quality care, even in the most resource-limited settings.

We're all participants in a multi-billion dollar mistake. The World Health Organization throws down a staggering statistic: over 50% of all medicines are prescribed, dispensed, or sold inappropriately. The sheer scale of this problem demands a solution, and it exists, conceptually, in a framework known as "Rational Use of Medication" (RUM). More than just a lofty ideal, it’s a practical approach, and tech startups on the ground, like Medrafa in Ethiopia, are transforming this ideal into tangible change.

## What is Rational Use of Medication (RUM)?

But what *is* "Rational Use of Medication," really? It sounds almost patronizing, as if we're being lectured on being "smart" about our health.

In essence, RUM boils down to this: ensuring the *right medicine* reaches the *right patient*, in the *right dose* and for the *right duration*, all while keeping costs as low as possible. It's about optimizing the entire medication process, from prescription to consumption.

Think of it like this: RUM is the difference between a master chef meticulously following a complex recipe, and a toddler gleefully tossing random ingredients from the fridge into a pot. Both involve ingredients and effort, but only one results in something beneficial.

The same principle applies to medication. When RUM is practiced, we see better health outcomes, a reduction in adverse effects, significant cost savings for both individuals and healthcare systems, and, critically, a slowdown in the development of antimicrobial resistance.

## A Brief History of RUM

Now, how did we arrive at this point, where such a seemingly simple concept is so poorly implemented? The history of medicine is a long and winding road, paved with good intentions but often shrouded in guesswork. For centuries, medical practices were based on tradition, anecdotal evidence, and a hefty dose of intuition.

It wasn't until the 1970s that a true wake-up call occurred. The WHO recognized the urgent need for a standardized list of "essential" medicines – medications considered the most effective and safe for addressing the most pressing health needs. The first "Model List" in 1977 was a revolutionary step, providing a framework for countries to develop their own national lists.

Then, in 1985, the Nairobi Conference officially defined "Rational Use of Medication," solidifying it as a global mission. You could almost see it as the Woodstock for smart medicine use, a pivotal moment when the world collectively acknowledged the need for a more systematic and evidence-based approach.

## The Challenges to Rational Medication Use

But why is it so damn *hard* to get this right? The devil, as always, is in the details. The path to rational medication use is fraught with challenges, ethical dilemmas, and outright controversy.

Consider the complexities of polypharmacy. We see it in the medicine cabinets of our aging relatives, a bewildering array of pills, each with its own potential side effects and interactions. It's a pharmacological minefield, where the risk of adverse events increases exponentially with each added medication.

Then there's the Antibiotic Apocalypse. The rampant overuse of antibiotics, often prescribed for viral infections against which they are completely ineffective, has fueled the rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, threatening to render many of our most powerful drugs useless.

The "a pill for every ill" mentality, where patients pressure doctors for prescriptions even when they're not medically necessary, further exacerbates the problem. We can’t ignore the influence of Big Pharma, either.

The ethical tightrope they walk, balancing profit motives with patient well-being, can lead to aggressive marketing tactics and financial incentives that unduly influence prescribing practices. And finally, there's the fundamental tension between a doctor's professional recommendation and a patient's right to choose – the delicate balance between paternalism and autonomy.

Amidst this complex landscape, innovative solutions are emerging. Enter Medrafa, an Ethiopian health-tech company tackling these challenges head-on.

Medrafa isn't just another Silicon Valley import; it's a homegrown solution, deeply rooted in the specific needs and realities of the Ethiopian healthcare system.

User reviews highlight the critical need for offline functionality, revealing the challenges of operating in areas with unreliable internet access. It's this commitment to addressing real-world constraints that sets Medrafa apart.

## The Future of RUM and Technology

Looking ahead, the future of RUM is inextricably linked to technology. We're on the cusp of a new era of personalized medicine, where pharmacogenomics allows us to tailor medications to an individual's unique genetic makeup.

Artificial intelligence is poised to revolutionize drug discovery, predict medication adherence, and identify dangerous drug interactions. We'll see the rise of smart pill bottles, ingestible sensors, and sophisticated apps that provide real-time feedback and support to patients. Medrafa is already leveraging AI and building the interconnected system necessary to realize this future.

Rational Use of Medication isn't merely a dry policy guideline; it's a crucial battle for our health, our financial well-being, and the future of medicine. While global organizations like the WHO play a vital role in setting standards and promoting best practices, the real change is happening on the front lines, driven by innovative, locally-aware companies like Medrafa.

The future of medicine isn't just about discovering the next blockbuster drug; it's about using the medications we already have, rationally and effectively. It's about transforming that multi-billion dollar mistake into a multi-billion dollar opportunity to improve lives around the world.
